newsitem.title: BURUNDI: U.N. envoy sees "Marshall Plan" for Great Lakes.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy sees "Marshall Plan" for Great Lakes.

text.p: United Nations and Organisation of African Unity joint envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said on Friday that aid was needed for the Great Lakes region to end warfare spurred by poverty.

"I am going to mobilise resources for the development of the Great Lakes and I envisage a mini-Marshall Plan for the region," Sahnoun told reporters after talks with Burundi's military ruler Pierre Buyoya who seized power in an army coup last July.
After World War II the United States funded the Marshall Plan aid programme to help war-ravaged Europe develop again.

Sahnoun also said he did not immediately envisage an international peacekeeping force being sent to Zaire, where the army is battling rebels who have taken control of a strip of territory in the country's east.
But he said this could change following talks with the groups involved in the fighting that broke out in October. Sahnoun is expected to have talks in Rwanda on Saturday before flying to Zaire.

Sahnoun, who was appointed last month, said he would examine the economic and transport embargo on Burundi imposed by regional states shortly after the coup in an attempt to push Buyoya to open peace talks with Hutu rebels.

The Burundian military-appointed government has campaigned for sanctions to be lifted and aid agencies have said delays in excluding aid from the embargo are hurting only the needy, not the politicians.

Sahnoun, the first joint envoy of the United Nations and the OAU, arrived in Africa on Tuesday at his Nairobi headquarters for his mission to bring peace to the region including Zaire, Burundi and Rwanda.

Since his appointment, Sahnoun has spoken of the need for a comprehensive solution to the Great Lakes crises. But U.N. officials say he will need to tackle problems one by one before political conditions are suitable for an overall resolution.
